docs.title: The 8-Bit Home
docs.text:
An illustrated field guide · 1977–1987 The8-Bit Home

How beige boxes, rubber keys, cassette tapes and blinking cursors brought computing out of the laboratory—and taught a generation to make things.

Cover image · AI-generated editorial illustration · not documentary evidence

Start reading → Choose a reading trail

docs.title: The computer arrives at home
docs.text:
For a brief, unruly period, there was no settled idea of what a home computer should be. One company sold a complete machine with its own monitor and tape deck. Another supplied a tiny keyboard and expected the family television to do the rest. Some machines were serious schoolroom instruments; others smuggled powerful game hardware into the house under the respectable label “computer.”

That variety is the heart of this book. These machines did more than compete on memory, color, or price. Each offered a different answer to a larger question: what might an ordinary person do with a computer?

10 yearsFROM THE 1977 TRINITY TO THE MATURE 8-BIT ERA 15+ machinesFROM THE PET AND APPLE II TO THE CPC 2 continentsDIFFERENT MARKETS, SHARED CURIOSITY

docs.title: Pick a doorway
docs.text:
SinclairZX80 · ZX81 · ZX SPECTRUMMinimal hardware, maximum imagination. CommodorePET · VIC-20 · COMMODORE 64Vertical integration meets mass culture. Atari400 · 800Arcade thinking enters the living room. AcornBBC MICROA television project becomes a classroom standard. AppleII · IIe · IIcAn expandable computer becomes a durable platform. AmstradCPC 464 · 664 · 6128Everything you need, all in one box.

A note on names

The requested “ZX 80,” “ZX 81,” and “Spectrum” appear here under their usual names: ZX80, ZX81, and ZX Spectrum. “Apple Inc” is treated as the likely machine name Apple IIc, alongside the Apple II and IIe.

docs.title: What made the era special?
docs.text:
The limits were visible. You could count memory in kilobytes, hear storage as an angry whistle, and watch the screen redraw. Yet those constraints invited participation. The boot screen was often a programming prompt. Magazines printed software as pages of code. The distance between using a computer and changing what it did could be one line of BASIC.

This is not a catalogue of winners. It is a tour of competing ideas: cheap access, polished engineering, classroom networks, arcade graphics, speech, expandability, and the convenience of a monitor bundled in the carton.

Begin with the shape of the revolution →

docs.title: How to read this book
docs.text: Orientation · 6 minute read

docs.title: How to read this book
docs.text:
A home computer was never just a smaller office machine. It was a proposition: buy this box and discover what computing could mean in your own life.

Between the late 1970s and the middle of the 1980s, manufacturers tried nearly every version of that proposition. Commodore sold integration and scale. Sinclair drove price and component count downward. Atari began with custom chips that made color and motion natural. Acorn made speed, connectivity, and teaching central to the BBC Micro. Apple cultivated a platform that could keep changing. Texas Instruments brought unusual 16-bit architecture to a mass-market fight. Amstrad removed the intimidating hunt for a compatible display and cassette recorder by putting a complete system in one carton.

docs.title: Three lenses
docs.text:
Each machine chapter uses three lenses rather than pretending that specifications tell the whole story.

01 · The object

Case, keyboard, display, storage, expansion and the physical ritual of getting started.

02 · The invitation

Who the machine imagined its user to be: pupil, hobbyist, family, gamer, or small-business owner.

03 · The afterlife

The software, communities and habits that survived after the hardware left shops.

docs.title: Specifications need context
docs.text:
A number such as “64 KB” looks definitive but can mislead. Memory might be shared with video hardware, hidden behind ROM, unavailable to BASIC, or expanded through a peripheral. Clock speeds cannot be compared cleanly across processor families. Display capabilities depended on modes, television standards, and clever software tricks. Prices varied by country and changed rapidly during fierce competition.

For that reason, the specification cards describe representative launch-era configurations. They are signposts, not scoreboards. The machine matrix makes variations explicit.

docs.title: The sound of software
docs.text:
For many owners, a program began as sound. Domestic cassette tape was slow but cheap, familiar, and widely available. Loading required patience: start the tape, type a command, adjust the volume, and wait while pulses became bytes. Floppy disks offered speed and random access, but drives could cost as much as a budget computer.

PRESS PLAY ON TAPE SEARCHING... FOUND "ADVENTURE" LOADING ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓░░░

That inconvenience shaped culture. Programs were small. Loading screens became an art form. Compilation cassettes made software feel like recorded music. Typing a listing from a magazine bypassed loading altogether—provided you found every mistake.

docs.title: A transatlantic story
docs.text:
The “home computer” meant different things in different markets. In the United States, Apple II machines became deeply associated with schools, Atari connected computing to videogames, and the TI-99/4A fought a punishing retail battle. In Britain, low-cost Sinclair machines, the BBC Computer Literacy Project, and a dense software press made programming unusually public. Across Europe, Amstrad’s complete packages lowered the friction of buying a system.

The borders were porous. MOS Technology’s 6502 appeared inside American and British machines. Microsoft BASIC turned up in many competing systems. Ideas, games and programming techniques moved wherever tapes, disks, magazines and modems could carry them.

Read non-linearly

Follow the chapters in order for a chronological arc, or jump directly to a machine you remember. Explore the book offers machine, year and experience trails; the timeline and glossary are designed to remain open in a second tab.

docs.title: What this edition covers
docs.text:
The core cast is the Commodore PET and 64; Radio Shack TRS-80 Model I; Sinclair ZX80, ZX81 and Spectrum; BBC Micro; Atari 400 and 800; Apple II, IIe and IIc; TI-99/4A; and Amstrad CPC. The VIC-20 and several related systems appear where they illuminate the story. The Model III appears briefly as the TRS-80’s afterlife.

This is a selective, transatlantic starting point rather than a complete map of home computing. The older chapters formed the original edition and are now being audited against a fuller claim-level sourcing and review process. The TRS-80 Model I spotlight is the first chapter completed under that expanded cycle. Scope & method explains how sources, uncertainty, generated illustration, corrections and review dates are handled.

docs.title: Corrections & source leads
docs.text: About · Corrigibility

docs.title: Corrections & source leads
docs.text:
A trustworthy history must be correctable. If a date, specification, attribution, quotation, caption or interpretation looks wrong, show us the page and the evidence.

Report a correction or source lead View open reports

docs.title: Published corrections
docs.text:
Record Page Earlier text Corrected text Corrected Edition note correction:2026-001 Home page “3 continents” “2 continents” 20 September 2026 Corrected before the Operating Edition

Corrections found during final review are recorded even when they are fixed before an edition is released. This makes the effect of review visible without implying that the incorrect wording necessarily appeared on the public site.

docs.title: What to include
docs.text:
A useful report gives:

  • the page URL and the exact sentence, table row or image concerned;
  • what may be wrong, incomplete or too certain;
  • an inspectable source and the relevant page, object number or timestamp;
  • the machine, revision, country and date involved, when they matter; and
  • any conflict of interest or uncertainty that could help the review.

Please link to material rather than uploading a scan or photograph unless you have the right to share it. Do not include private personal information.

A source lead is welcome even when it does not prove a correction by itself. Period manuals, catalogues and institutional records usually carry more weight for specifications and dates than an unattributed summary. A community post or memory can identify a question that deserves research without becoming the sole support for a consequential claim.

docs.title: What happens next
docs.text:
The report is triaged, checked against the current page and compared with the best available evidence. A reviewer may ask for a more precise locator, seek an independent source, narrow the claim, or record a genuine disagreement between sources.

If the evidence supports a change, the correction enters the appropriate review path before publication. A correction to one specification may affect a table, timeline and several chapters, so the review looks for every place that repeats the claim. Material changes are recorded in the edition history.

Submitting a report does not transfer authorship of the page, guarantee that a proposed interpretation will be accepted, or turn private correspondence into evidence. Decisions should be explained from the sources rather than from a contributor's identity or number of reactions.

docs.title: Three different ways to contribute
docs.text:
• Use a content proposal for a missing machine, community, object or theme.
  • Use a correction or source lead for a statement already published or for stronger evidence relevant to it.
  • Use a recollection for a personal memory of using, buying, teaching, repairing or sharing a machine. Recollections remain labelled testimony and are not silently converted into general historical fact.

The contribution guide explains all three routes.

Read how evidence is assessed →

docs.title: Editions & updates
docs.text: About · Publication history

docs.title: Editions & updates
docs.text: This is a living publication, but it should not change invisibly. The repository preserves its history; this page explains how readers can interpret that history.

docs.title: What counts as an edition
docs.text:
An edition is an approved state of the whole book: prose, sources, images, navigation and reference pages taken together. A release record identifies the exact source state used to build the published site. Generated site files are outputs, not a second manuscript to edit by hand.

Changes fall into three practical groups:

Change Examples Review path Editorial addition A new chapter, substantial rewrite, new visual program or changed interpretation Full research, editorial, factual, visual and reader review as applicable Factual correction A wrong date, model, attribution, quotation, specification or unsupported claim Evidence check, impact review and correction record Maintenance Broken link replacement, accessibility repair or formatting fix that does not alter meaning Automated checks plus editorial inspection where meaning could change

A quiet copy edit need not become a new historical interpretation. A changed claim must not be disguised as a copy edit.

docs.title: Operating Edition — 25 September 2026
docs.text:
This edition adds the reader-facing structure needed to keep the book inspectable and improving:

  • an Explore page with machine, year and experience reading trails;
  • public pages for editorial method, editions, corrections and image credits;
  • separate contribution routes for proposals, corrections or source leads, and clearly labelled recollections; and
  • optimized WebP delivery for the current editorial illustrations, while larger source masters remain available for review and future derivatives.

The intended immutable release tag is edition-2026-09-25. That link becomes resolvable only when the publisher has completed the release gates and published the GitHub release; naming it here does not claim that the release already exists.

docs.title: The current body of work
docs.text:
The publication contains an orientation, narrative chapters and reference pages covering the 1977 generation, Sinclair, Commodore, Atari, the BBC Micro, Apple II family, TI-99/4A, Amstrad CPC, everyday use, software cultures and legacies. The TRS-80 Model I is the first machine spotlight completed under the expanded research-to-reader workflow.

The earlier chapters are being audited in place. Until an individual page carries a completed review record under the newer process, readers should not assume that it has the same claim-level sourcing or visual review as the TRS-80 spotlight. Scope & method explains the difference.

docs.title: Reading review dates
docs.text:
A last reviewed date means the page's claims and citations were deliberately rechecked on that date. It does not mean that every external source was created or updated then. A formatting change should not reset the historical review date; a substantive factual review should.

Review dates will be added as chapters complete the upgraded process. The absence of one is useful information: it means the page belongs to the legacy set still awaiting a recorded full review.

docs.title: Coverage status for this edition
docs.text:
This table reflects the publication register for the current operating edition. “Not recorded” means no completed fact-review date is present; it does not mean that no one has ever read or checked the page.

Coverage Pages Status Last fact review Reader review TRS-80 Model I spotlight chapters/trs-80 Ready 20 September 2026 92/100 Home, Explore, Contribute and the four About pages 7 pages Ready 25 September 2026 89/100 Orientation and all other narrative chapters 11 pages Legacy Not recorded Not recorded Timeline, machine matrix, collecting guide, glossary and sources 5 pages Legacy Not recorded Not recorded

Ready means the recorded expanded workflow is complete. Legacy means the page predates the expanded record and remains queued for audit; it is not a judgment that every statement on the page is wrong.

docs.title: Inspecting change
docs.text:
The public Git history shows the exact files changed over time. Edition notes summarize reader-relevant changes; the commit history supplies the finer audit trail. Accepted factual corrections should identify the affected page, the old and new account, and the evidence used.

No history can guarantee that the current text is error-free. It makes errors and editorial choices easier to find, discuss and repair.

Report a correction → Read the editorial method →

docs.text: Images can explain, evoke and mislead. This register identifies the published editorial images and states when a scene is illustrative rather than documentary.

docs.title: Current editorial illustrations
docs.text:
The present content pages use three original AI-generated editorial illustrations. They are not archival photographs, surviving advertisements or evidence of an exact historical arrangement.

Image Appears on Status and intended use cover-home-computers.webp Home AI-generated cover illustration for this edition; an atmospheric entry to the book, not a record of one room or collection trs80-retail-desk.webp TRS-80 Model I AI-generated illustration of a plausible late-1977 retail demonstration; not an archival photograph or exact hardware reconstruction trs80-expansion-system.webp TRS-80 Model I AI-generated illustration of the external, expanding Model I system; not an archival photograph or exact hardware reconstruction

The site also uses a small interface icon. It is decorative site furniture, not historical evidence.

docs.title: How to read future images
docs.text:
Every substantial visual should declare which role it serves:

  • Documentary image: an identified artifact, photograph or scan, with a source, date where known, rights status and any relevant crop or restoration.
  • Explanatory graphic: a diagram or comparison created for the publication. The caption identifies simplifications, and the same essential information is available without relying on color or vision.
  • Illustrative image: a reconstruction or atmospheric scene. AI generation, if used, is disclosed next to the image. The image cannot substantiate a historical claim.

Alt text describes useful visual information; captions explain provenance and historical limits. Decorative images should be marked as such rather than given performative descriptions. A rights-uncertain image is not published merely because it is easy to find online.

If an image appears misidentified, anachronistic or inadequately disclosed, report it as a correction.

Read the complete editorial method →

docs.title: Scope & method
docs.text: About · Evidence and editorial method

docs.title: Scope & method
docs.text: The 8-Bit Home is a selective field guide to the formative home-computer years. It joins technical detail to the ordinary experience of buying, connecting, programming, playing with and expanding a machine.

docs.title: What belongs here
docs.text:
The main story runs from 1977 to 1987 and currently concentrates on machines and experiences in the United States and western Europe, especially Britain. That is a boundary, not a claim that home computing happened only there. Systems, markets and communities beyond the present coverage are important gaps for future research.

The book follows three recurring questions:

  • The object: What did the machine, its storage, display, documentation and expansion system ask someone to handle?
  • The invitation: Who was expected to use it, and what could they reasonably do in the first hour or first months?
  • The afterlife: Which software, communities, skills and preservation work continued beyond the original sale?

Specifications are always qualified by model, region and revision where the evidence supports that precision. A launch configuration is not every configuration, an advertised capability is not proof of everyday use, and a manufacturer's date may describe an announcement rather than immediate local availability.

docs.title: How we use sources
docs.text:
Different sources answer different questions. We identify the class and its limits instead of treating every link as equal.

Source class Best used for Questions we still ask Period material: manuals, catalogues, advertisements, software and reviews Configuration, contemporary language, price and intended use Which edition, market and revision? Is this a promotional claim? Museums, libraries and institutional archives Object provenance, collection records and historical context Does the record describe one specimen or a whole product family? Scholarship and researched books Historical argument, social context and competing interpretations Which evidence and geography support the argument? Specialist archives and databases Technical depth, rare documents and promising leads Can a consequential claim be traced to an inspectable source? Named interviews and oral histories Experience, motive and memory Is the account first-hand, dated and clearly attributed? Forums, social posts, video and community recollections Questions, leads and lived experience Can the factual parts be corroborated? Is the memory representative or personal?

Community knowledge is invaluable, but confidence and popularity are not evidence. A recollection can remain useful while being clearly labelled as a recollection.

docs.title: From question to publication
docs.text:
A substantial addition begins with a bounded brief and research questions. A research pass collects inspectable sources and records contradictions. A writer then works from that evidence; separate editorial, factual and citation checks challenge the draft. Visuals receive their own accuracy, provenance, accessibility and rights review. The rendered page must build successfully and pass an independent reader review before release.

No writer approves their own work. Automated checks can find broken links, missing metadata and build failures, but they cannot settle disputed history, grant image rights or decide that uncertain evidence has become certain. Those decisions remain editorial responsibilities.

docs.title: Uncertainty is part of the record
docs.text:
Surviving sources disagree. Product families contain quiet revisions. Prices move, regional bundles differ, and memories compress events. When evidence does not support one clean answer, the page should narrow the claim, attribute the difference or state that the question remains unresolved.

Important claims should have a nearby source. Supporting records note the specific page, object, timestamp, model or market where possible. A source list is a route back to the evidence, not a substitute for explaining what that evidence supports.

docs.title: Visual evidence and illustration
docs.text:
The site distinguishes three kinds of image:

  • Documentary: an archival photograph, scan or image of an identified artifact. Its date, holding source and reuse status must be recorded.
  • Explanatory: a diagram or comparison made to clarify a configuration or relationship. Important information must also be available in text.
  • Illustrative: an artistic reconstruction or atmospheric scene, including AI-generated art. It must be labelled and must never prove what a machine, shop or historical event looked like.

An attractive image can still contain an anachronism. Captions therefore say what an illustration is intended to convey and where exact reconstruction should not be inferred. See Image credits for the assets in this edition.

docs.title: A publication being upgraded
docs.text:
The newer TRS-80 Model I chapter was produced with the full research, visual, edit and reader-review cycle. The older chapters formed the original edition and do not yet all have the same claim-level evidence, visual provenance and review record. They remain useful introductions while they are audited and upgraded. This distinction is deliberate and will not be hidden behind a blanket claim that every page has already passed the newer standard.

As pages are reviewed, their scope, evidence and revision notes will be made more explicit. Material changes belong in the edition history, and errors can be reported through the corrections process.

docs.title: Collector's field notes
docs.text: Reference · Care & preservation

docs.title: Collector’s field notes
docs.text: A vintage computer is an artifact and an electrical device. Preserve its history, but do not assume age has made it harmless.

docs.title: Before power-on
docs.text:
Unknown power supplies need inspection

Old power supplies can fail in ways that damage irreplaceable custom chips. Do not connect an unknown machine simply to “see if it works.” Have the supply and computer checked by someone competent with that model.

  • Confirm the exact model, region and required voltage.
  • Inspect cables, plugs and boards for damage, corrosion or modifications.
  • Research model-specific failure modes before applying power.
  • Treat mains-voltage sections and CRT displays as hazardous even when unplugged.
  • Never work inside a CRT without the appropriate training.

docs.title: Buy the story, not only the box
docs.text: Packaging, receipts, manuals, homemade cables, labeled tapes and school asset tags are historical evidence. Ask where a machine came from and photograph its condition before cleaning. A name scratched beneath a case may matter more to future interpretation than cosmetic perfection.

docs.title: Clean conservatively
docs.text: Start with a soft brush and controlled methods. Test any cleaner on a hidden area. Avoid aggressive “restoration” that removes texture, labels, patina or manufacturing marks. Keep replaced parts with the machine and document every repair.

docs.title: Preserve media in layers
docs.text:
1. Keep the original cassette, disk or cartridge in stable conditions.
  2. Create a digital image with suitable, non-destructive hardware.
  3. Record labels, checksums, format, hardware and software used.
  4. Make at least two verified copies in different locations.
  5. Respect copyright and personal data when sharing an image.

docs.title: Choose a use strategy
docs.text:
There is no single correct balance between operation and conservation.

Original experienceDaily driverResearch copy

Use period displays, storage and controllers. This preserves timing, sound, handling and setup, but places wear on old components.

Use a tested modern supply, video adapter and solid-state storage interface. Keep original parts labeled and reversible where possible.

Use emulation for repeatability, screenshots and software comparison. Record emulator version and settings as part of the research method.

The best collections are legible. A future owner should be able to tell what is original, what was repaired, what was replaced, and why.

docs.title: Contribute
docs.text: Contribute · Three routes

docs.title: Help the field guide grow
docs.text:
A missing subject, a wrong specification and a memory of using a machine are three different kinds of contribution. Choosing the right route lets each receive the evidence and review it needs.

Propose new coverage Report a correction or source lead Share a recollection View the ranked backlog

docs.title: Choose the right route
docs.text:
Route Use it when… How it is treated Content proposal A machine, community, object, place or practice is missing or deserves a deeper treatment An editorial candidate, ranked for reader value, distinctiveness, evidence, fit and feasibility Correction or source lead A published claim, caption or table may be wrong, incomplete or too certain—or you have stronger evidence A factual report to verify against the page and all other places that repeat the claim Recollection You want to describe buying, using, teaching, repairing or sharing a machine Attributed personal testimony, kept distinct from general historical fact and corroborated where factual claims require it

Do not reshape a correction as a popular vote or a memory as a universal claim. All three can improve the publication precisely because they do different work.

docs.title: What makes an idea useful
docs.text:
A strong proposal identifies more than a favorite machine. It explains the reader promise: what someone will understand after reading the new material that the current book does not yet make clear. The form asks for:

  • a proposed title and one-sentence reader promise;
  • missing or incorrect coverage and the relevant current page;
  • the period, region and exact machines, models or revisions involved;
  • up to three inspectable sources;
  • the benefit for a curious newcomer;
  • accessibility needs or useful visual approaches; and
  • overlaps, conflicts or duplicate coverage you have noticed.

Please link to sources rather than uploading scans or images whose rights are unclear. Do not include private personal information. A source suggestion helps research begin; it does not by itself validate a historical claim.

docs.title: How proposals, discussion and voting work
docs.text:
Readers may use GitHub reactions on an idea issue as a lightweight preference signal. Reactions show interest, not factual accuracy, and they do not create a publication commitment. Contributor identity and popularity are never evidence for a claim.

On a regular editorial cadence, moderators may merge duplicates and record a dated snapshot of reaction counts in the public ranked backlog. These are periodic snapshots, not live reaction totals. Each candidate is then assessed for reader value, distinctiveness, available evidence, fit with the book’s 1977–1987 scope, and production feasibility; the reader scorecard makes the current scoring components inspectable. Votes inform the reader-value part of that judgment; they cannot override source quality, regional or model precision, accessibility, rights, editorial capacity or the safety of the work.

An idea may be marked as needing sources, ready for research, shortlisted, accepted or declined with a reason. Status can change when stronger evidence or a better-defined scope appears.

docs.title: Corrections and recollections
docs.text:
A correction report should name the page and passage, explain the concern and give an inspectable locator when possible. The corrections page explains how evidence is checked and how material changes enter the edition history.

A recollection should identify the approximate place, period and machine or revision where known. Say which details you remember directly and which are later interpretation. Publication is not guaranteed, and private information should not be included. Memories can illuminate everyday experience without being treated as proof that everyone used a machine in the same way.

docs.title: Moderation and care
docs.text:
Moderators remove spam, harassment, personal data and rights-problematic uploads. They may edit labels, request clarification, check links, narrow a proposal or merge duplicate issues. Discussion should address the proposed coverage and evidence, not the identity of the contributor.

Acceptance starts an editorial cycle; it does not send issue text directly into the book. Research, drafting, visual review, editing, a strict build and an independent reader rating remain separate stages. Historical uncertainty and regional or revision differences will be preserved rather than smoothed away.

Browse existing content ideas Read our scope and method

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Reference · Terms

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
8-bit A broad label for systems whose CPU commonly processes eight bits at a time. It describes an era and architecture family, not a complete measure of ability.

BASIC A programming language designed for accessibility. Many home computers opened directly into a BASIC interpreter, making it both interface and development tool.

Bit / byte / kilobyte A bit is a binary digit. A byte is usually eight bits. Contemporary advertising often used “K” for 1,024 bytes of memory.

Cartridge A plug-in module containing ROM and sometimes extra hardware. It loads instantly and is physically robust but costs more to manufacture than tape or disk.

CPU The central processing unit: the chip that executes program instructions. Its clock rate alone does not determine whole-system performance.

CRT Cathode-ray tube, the display technology used in televisions and monitors of the period. CRTs can retain dangerous voltages and require specialist handling.

Datassette Commodore’s dedicated cassette storage device and interface.

Demo scene A creative community centered on real-time audiovisual programs that showcase technical and artistic skill.

Floppy disk Magnetic removable storage offering faster access and greater flexibility than cassette. Common home-computer formats included 5.25, 3.5 and 3-inch disks.

Machine code Instructions executed directly by a processor, generally faster and more compact than interpreted BASIC but harder to write and less portable.

PAL / NTSC Television standards used in different regions. Their timing and color systems affect display output, game speed and sometimes CPU clock rates.

RAM / ROM RAM is working memory that loses its contents without power. ROM retains fixed software such as BASIC, startup code or an operating environment.

RF output A radio-frequency signal that lets a computer connect through a television’s aerial input. Convenient, though usually less clear than a monitor connection.

Sprite A hardware-supported movable graphic independent of the main background. Names vary: Atari used “player/missile graphics.”

Z80 / 6502 Two influential 8-bit processor families found across many otherwise incompatible home computers.

docs.title: Machine matrix
docs.text: Reference · Specifications

docs.title: Machine matrix
docs.text:
Specifications describe representative launch models. Clock rates vary by region in systems synchronized to PAL or NTSC video; usable memory differs from installed RAM; later revisions may change cases, ROMs, boards or ports.

docs.title: Family resemblance
docs.text:
Three processor lineages dominate the table. The 6502 family connects PET, Apple, Atari, BBC and Commodore systems, even though their graphics, sound and operating environments differ profoundly. The Z80 family links the TRS-80, Sinclair and Amstrad, as well as many systems outside this book. Texas Instruments stands apart with the TMS9900.

That is a reminder that the CPU does not define the experience alone. Custom chips, memory architecture, ROM software, display hardware, ports, keyboards, storage and developer culture matter just as much.

docs.text: This e-book is a narrative introduction, not a service manual. Dates and technical details were checked against museum records, institutional archives and period documentation. Configurations changed across regions and revisions; the machine matrix deliberately uses representative launch-era specifications.

docs.title: Reading the sources critically
docs.text:
Manufacturer literature explains intended use but naturally promotes the product. Contemporary reviews reveal first impressions but may contain errors. Museum records offer curatorial context but sometimes describe one specimen rather than every revision. Community archives preserve extraordinary detail, yet should be cross-checked for consequential claims.

The most rewarding research combines them: manual, machine, software, magazine, advertisement, oral history and surviving everyday evidence.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text: Reference · Chronology

docs.title: A decade on the desk
docs.text:
The machines overlap more than memory suggests. This timeline places key launches beside the platform changes they enabled.

Dates are not endings

A launch year marks a beginning. Models remained on sale for different periods across regions, and software communities frequently outlived retail availability by decades.

docs.title: 1976 · Apple-1
docs.text: Steve Wozniak’s assembled board helps launch Apple Computer. It still expects its buyer to supply the surrounding hardware.

docs.title: 1977 · PET, Apple II, TRS-80
docs.text: Radio Shack introduces the TRS-80 Microcomputer System on 3 August and offers a US bundle of keyboard computer, monitor and cassette recorder; availability rolls out through selected stores.

docs.title: 1979 · Atari 400/800 and TI-99/4
docs.text: Atari emphasizes custom graphics and sound; Texas Instruments introduces an unusual 16-bit CPU to the home market.

docs.title: 1980 · Sinclair ZX80 and TRS-80 Model III
docs.text: A tiny British machine turns aggressive simplicity into a design strategy, while Radio Shack consolidates much of the expandable Model I system into the self-contained Model III.

docs.title: 1981 · ZX81, VIC-20, TI-99/4A, BBC Micro
docs.text: Low prices expand the audience while the BBC/Acorn partnership builds a more ambitious educational system.

docs.title: 1982 · ZX Spectrum and Commodore 64
docs.text: Two defining mass-market platforms arrive with very different balances of cost, color, sound and design.

docs.title: 1983 · Apple IIe
docs.text: Apple refines compatibility and strengthens a platform already established in homes, schools and businesses.

docs.title: 1984 · Apple IIc and Amstrad CPC 464
docs.text: The IIc integrates the Apple II experience; Amstrad sells a complete computer, storage and monitor package.

docs.title: 1985 · Amstrad CPC 664/6128
docs.text: Integrated disk drives and, in the 6128, expanded memory mature the CPC line.

docs.title: 1987 · The 8-bit afterlife begins
docs.text: 16-bit systems are increasingly prominent, yet established 8-bit families continue selling, publishing and evolving.

docs.title: The 1977 generation
docs.text: Chapter 01 · 8 minute read

docs.title: The 1977 generation
docs.text:
Before 1977, owning a microcomputer usually meant joining a technical subculture. During 1977, three very different machines made “personal computer” look like a durable product category.

The Commodore PET 2001, Apple II, and Radio Shack TRS-80 Model I are often grouped as a trio. The label is useful so long as it does not flatten their differences. Their makers came from calculators and semiconductors, hobbyist electronics, and nationwide retail. They agreed on very little beyond the fact that a computer could belong to an individual.

docs.title: PET: computer as appliance
docs.text:
The first PET 2001 placed processor, memory, keyboard, cassette storage and a nine-inch monochrome display into one angular metal enclosure. It looked closer to laboratory equipment than to a toy. Lift the top and it opened like a car hood—a memorable detail on a machine otherwise designed to feel complete.

MOS 6502CPU · ABOUT 1 MHZ 4 or 8 KBEARLY PET 2001 RAM OPTIONS All-in-oneDISPLAY + KEYBOARD + CASSETTE

The small “chiclet” keyboard was striking and divisive. Its compact keys helped the PET fit neatly beneath its display, but frustrated touch typists. The built-in Datassette reinforced the appliance idea: no search for a compatible recorder, no mysterious television tuning. Switch on and BASIC was waiting.

Commodore’s purchase of MOS Technology mattered as much as the case. It gave the company access to the 6502 and to engineers including Chuck Peddle. That control of key components later helped Commodore compete aggressively on price.

docs.title: Apple II: computer as platform
docs.text:
The Apple II took another path. It arrived as a finished consumer object—with a molded case, keyboard, power supply and color graphics—but its removable lid and expansion slots made incompleteness a virtue. Owners and other companies could extend it.

Steve Wozniak’s design extracted surprising behavior from economical hardware. Color graphics made games persuasive. Expansion enabled disk controllers, printers, memory cards, communications, and specialized laboratory or business hardware. When VisiCalc arrived, the same computer that played games became a reason for a small business to buy a microcomputer.

The Apple II’s enduring trick was not a single feature. It was leaving enough room—electrical, physical, and commercial—for other people’s ideas.

docs.title: TRS-80: computer as retail product
docs.text: Radio Shack paired its Z80-based computer with a monitor, cassette recorder, documentation and a staged path to memory, interfaces and disk. Its distinctive idea extended beyond the hardware: the retailer presented ordering, accessories and support as parts of the system, while warning that early stock was limited to selected stores. The TRS-80 Model I spotlight follows that path from the 1977 Level I package to the integrated Model III.

docs.title: Why this moment mattered
docs.text:
None of these systems was the first personal computer. What changed was the package around the circuit board: case, keyboard, language, documentation, distribution, software, support, and a story about who should own one.

The patterns established here recur throughout this book:

  • Integration: make the machine feel complete and approachable.
  • Expansion: leave room for an ecosystem to grow.
  • Distribution: meet buyers where they already shop.
  • A language at power-on: turn curiosity into a first program immediately.

The home-computer boom that followed did not choose one pattern. It recombined all four, often at much lower prices.

Museum record

The Smithsonian dates the PET’s introduction to 1977 and describes its 1 MHz 6502, integrated cassette, small display and 4 KB launch configuration. See the PET 2001 collection record.

Next: the TRS-80 turns retail into a feature →

docs.title: Amstrad CPC — the complete package
docs.text: Chapter 08 · 8 minute read

docs.title: Amstrad CPC — the complete package
docs.text:
By 1984, the home-computer market was crowded. Amstrad’s answer was not a radically new purpose. It was a radically tidy purchase.

The CPC 464 bundled a keyboard-computer with an integrated cassette deck and a dedicated monitor. Buyers chose green-screen or color, carried the cartons home, connected a small number of cables, and had a matched system. No family television needed to be occupied; no cassette recorder needed to be tested for compatibility.

docs.title: Integration as the innovation
docs.text:
The machine used familiar components: a Z80A processor, 64 KB of RAM, a video system built around the 6845 display controller, and AY sound. Yet the package changed the experience. The power supply was in the monitor. The cassette deck was built into the keyboard unit. Locomotive BASIC was capable and ready at startup.

CPC 4641984 · 64 KB + CASSETTE CPC 6641985 · 64 KB + 3-INCH DISK CPC 61281985 · 128 KB + 3-INCH DISK

The three primary display modes traded resolution for color. This gave software authors meaningful options: crisp text and detailed graphics at one extreme, chunkier pixels and a broader palette at the other. The results were visually distinct from both the Spectrum’s attribute system and the C64’s sprite-led strengths.

docs.title: From cassette to disk
docs.text:
The CPC 664 replaced the cassette deck with a compact three-inch disk drive. The CPC 6128 followed quickly with 128 KB of RAM and became the enduring disk model. The unusual disk format was convenient and robust but more expensive and less ubiquitous than 3.5- or 5.25-inch media.

CP/M support gave the disk systems access to a world of business and utility software beyond games. As with many home computers, the border between “serious” and “entertainment” use depended less on the machine than on peripherals, software, and the patience of its owner.

docs.title: A strong regional identity
docs.text:
The CPC found particular success in Britain, France, Spain and Germany. It received original software as well as conversions from Spectrum and C64 titles. Poor conversions sometimes failed to use its capabilities; careful ones gave the machine a visual and sonic identity of its own.

Amstrad demonstrated that reducing purchase anxiety could be as valuable as a headline feature. The CPC was a system rather than a puzzle: computer, storage and display designed to arrive together.

What CPC means

CPC stands for Colour Personal Computer. In the 464 name, the “4” refers to cassette storage and “64” to 64 KB of RAM; the later 6128 paired disk storage with 128 KB.

Next: living with 8 bits →

docs.title: Apple II family — a platform grows up
docs.text: Chapter 06 · 10 minute read

docs.title: Apple II family — a platform grows up
docs.text: The Apple II did not remain one machine. It became a compatible family whose changes reveal how the personal computer moved from enthusiast object to institution.

docs.title: Apple II: color and slots
docs.text:
Introduced in 1977, the original Apple II paired a 6502 processor with color graphics, a built-in keyboard, a plastic case and eight expansion slots. Compared with a bare hobbyist board, it looked finished. Compared with a sealed appliance, it was radically open.

That combination attracted both players and problem-solvers. Expansion cards added serial connections, printers, extra memory, sound, alternative processors, and laboratory interfaces. Disk II, designed with an economical controller, made floppy storage a defining part of the platform. VisiCalc showed that software could justify the purchase of the hardware.

docs.title: Apple IIe: compatibility as a feature
docs.text:
Released in 1983, the Apple IIe consolidated circuitry, improved the keyboard, and made capabilities that had once required add-ons easier to obtain. Its name promised enhancement rather than revolution. That was valuable to schools and owners with investments in software and peripherals.

Apple II1977The expandable foundation. Apple IIe1983Refinement, compatibility, institutional reach. Apple IIc1984A compact, integrated interpretation.

In American schools, the IIe became a familiar shared resource. Educational software ranged from drill-and-practice to simulations, writing tools, science activities and games. A computer lab created its own rituals: booking time, carrying floppy disks, and learning which machine had the reliable drive.

docs.title: Apple IIc: the compact turn
docs.text:
The 1984 Apple IIc reinterpreted the family as a slim, portable computer. It built in features commonly added to earlier models and integrated a floppy drive, while largely removing the internal expansion slots that defined the original. “Portable” still required an external display and power outlet, but the compact case anticipated a more appliance-like future.

This is why “Apple IIc” makes sense alongside the II and IIe: the three show a design philosophy changing over time. Expansion first made a market possible; integration later made the result easier to own.

docs.title: A platform measured in years
docs.text:
Longevity has compounding effects. Software libraries become deep. Repair knowledge circulates. Peripherals remain useful. Schools can add machines without abandoning lessons. Developers know what audience they can reach.

The Apple II family’s significance therefore lies in continuity as much as innovation. It bridged hobbyist clubs, homes, small businesses and formal education while graphical 16-bit systems emerged around it.

Compatibility is easy to overlook because it preserves yesterday. For an owner, a school, or a developer, that preservation can be the platform’s most important new feature.

Historical anchor

The Computer History Museum’s Apple timeline traces the Apple II from its West Coast Computer Faire debut. The museum’s broader computer timeline describes its complete package and long market life.

Next: Texas Instruments takes a different path →

docs.title: Atari 400 & 800 — custom-chip color
docs.text: Chapter 04 · 8 minute read

docs.title: Atari 400 & 800 — custom-chip color
docs.text:
Atari approached the home computer with experience no office-machine company possessed. It knew how movement, color and sound could make electronics feel immediate.

Announced in 1979, the Atari 400 and 800 shared a sophisticated architecture but presented different personalities. The lower-cost 400 used a pressure-sensitive membrane keyboard and a closed, friendly form. The 800 offered a proper keyboard, more accessible expansion and a more professional appearance. One leaned toward the game-playing family; the other could plausibly sit in a study.

docs.title: A team of specialist chips
docs.text:
The 6502 CPU did not work alone. Atari’s custom chips divided the visual and audio labor:

  • ANTIC interpreted display instructions and moved screen data.
  • CTIA/GTIA produced colors, player/missile graphics and collision features.
  • POKEY handled sound, timers, serial input/output and keyboard scanning.

This architecture made smooth scrolling, colorful displays and independent moving objects practical. The display list allowed different graphics modes to coexist vertically on one screen. In the hands of skilled programmers, it was less a fixed display than a script for constructing one line by line.

Atari 400MEMBRANE KEYBOARDDurable, approachable, game-forward. Atari 800FULL-TRAVEL KEYBOARDExpandable, twin cartridge slots, serious intent. SIOSERIAL INPUT/OUTPUTDaisy-chained intelligent peripherals.

docs.title: The peripheral chain
docs.text: Atari’s Serial Input/Output bus connected disk drives, printers, cassette recorders and modems in a daisy chain. Devices could identify themselves and communicate over a shared protocol. The result anticipated the convenience of later peripheral buses, although the connectors and ecosystem remained proprietary.

docs.title: Games, tools, and creative software
docs.text:
Atari’s arcade heritage was obvious, but the computer line was not merely a console with keys. Atari BASIC, word processors, telecommunications software, music tools and graphics packages all found users. Programs such as Eastern Front demonstrated how the same custom hardware that enabled arcade action could support ambitious strategy and simulation.

The machines also became important to early digital artists and demo makers. Color registers, display-list interrupts and player/missile graphics rewarded technical intimacy. A screen effect often began with understanding when the electron beam reached a particular line.

docs.title: Design tension
docs.text:
The membrane keyboard protected the Atari 400 from spills and rough hands, but made sustained typing unpleasant. The 800 solved that problem at a higher price. Together they expose a persistent home-computer dilemma: is the machine a durable family entertainment device or a general-purpose tool? Atari tried to serve both without building two unrelated platforms.

Historical anchor

The Computer History Museum dates the Atari 400 and 800 to 1979 and notes their improved graphics, sound, memory and expandability relative to Atari’s earlier console work. See the CHM timeline and its essay Game On.

Next: the BBC Micro enters the classroom →

docs.title: BBC Micro — a national classroom
docs.text: Chapter 05 · 9 minute read

docs.title: BBC Micro — a national classroom
docs.text:
The BBC Micro was part of something larger than a product launch: a coordinated attempt to make a country conversant with computing.

The BBC’s Computer Literacy Project joined television programs, educational material and an associated microcomputer. Acorn’s winning design became the BBC Micro, released around the launch of The Computer Programme in early 1982. It was more expensive than a Sinclair machine, but its keyboard, interfaces, performance and expandability suited repeated use in classrooms.

docs.title: Built to be explored
docs.text:
The BBC Micro used a fast 6502A processor and offered 16 KB in the Model A or 32 KB in the Model B. A row of red function keys gave the case a distinctive face. Numerous ports connected analog experiments, printers, disk drives, networks, user hardware and a second processor.

6502ACPU · 2 MHZ 16 / 32 KBMODEL A / MODEL B RAM BBC BASICSTRUCTURED FEATURES + ASSEMBLER EconetCLASSROOM NETWORKING

BBC BASIC was central to the proposition. It combined an approachable immediate mode with procedures, meaningful control structures and an inline assembler. Beginners could print a greeting; advanced users could move toward machine code without leaving the supplied environment.

10 MODE 7 20 PRINT TAB(8,5); "COMPUTER LITERACY" 30 FOR I%=1 TO 1000: NEXT 40 CLS 50 GOTO 20

docs.title: Television as documentation
docs.text:
The surrounding broadcasts treated computing as a subject with social and creative dimensions, not simply a lesson in operating one machine. Viewers saw programming, robotics, graphics, databases and the changing workplace. The computer gave abstract ideas a common practical target.

This coordination is difficult to imagine now. A broadcast could demonstrate a program, a book could print it, and viewers could run a version on the same machine at home, school, or a local computer club. The BBC’s surviving archive now lets modern visitors watch the programs and run many associated BBC Micro programs in a browser.

docs.title: The school network
docs.text:
Econet allowed multiple machines to share files and printers through a network. Networking was not unique to Acorn, but its presence in schools made concepts such as logins, shared storage and electronic messaging part of everyday computer education for some pupils.

The BBC Micro also supported “second processors” connected through its Tube interface. This unusually ambitious architecture let an external processor run applications while the original machine handled input and output. It expressed Acorn’s broader belief that a home or school computer could be a serious system.

docs.title: Legacy beyond the beige case
docs.text:
The machine’s educational footprint shaped careers, but its technical lineage also mattered. Acorn’s later work led toward the ARM processor architecture. The BBC Micro itself lives on through preservation projects, emulation, restored software and the continuing accessibility of BBC BASIC.

Watch and run the archive

The BBC Computer Literacy Project Archive holds 267 programs, thousands of categorized clips, and 166 BBC Micro programs used on screen. Its project history explains how the associated computer became part of the initiative.

Next: the Apple II becomes a family →

docs.title: Commodore — silicon for everyone
docs.text: Chapter 03 · 10 minute read

docs.title: Commodore — silicon for everyone
docs.text: Commodore understood that the computer business could be won in factories and shops as well as engineering labs. Owning chip technology let it turn sophisticated silicon into increasingly affordable machines.

docs.title: From PET to living room
docs.text:
The PET had established Commodore as a computer maker, but its integrated monitor and metal case suited schools and offices better than a television cabinet. The VIC-20, launched broadly in 1981, changed the setting. It used a friendly cream enclosure, color graphics, cartridge software, and a television for display. Its modest memory did not prevent it from becoming a genuine mass-market computer.

Commodore sold through channels beyond specialist computer shops. This was a crucial shift: a family could encounter a programmable computer in an ordinary retail environment, beside familiar consumer goods.

docs.title: Commodore 64: the long-lived compromise
docs.text:
Introduced in 1982, the Commodore 64 combined 64 KB of RAM with two defining custom chips. VIC-II handled color graphics, sprites and scrolling. SID made the machine a remarkable synthesizer as well as a computer. The familiar “breadbin” case held a full-travel keyboard and connected to televisions, monitors, cassette drives, disk drives, joysticks and cartridges.

MOS 6510CPU · APPROX. 1 MHZ, REGION-DEPENDENT 64 KBRAM · SHARED ADDRESS SPACE VIC-IICOLOR, SPRITES, SCROLLING SIDTHREE-VOICE SYNTHESIS

The specifications were only half the story. Commodore’s control of MOS Technology supported brutal price competition. Production scale kept the model on shelves for years. Longevity encouraged software publishers, hardware makers, user groups and magazines, which made the computer safer to buy, which in turn expanded the market again.

docs.title: The disk drive that was nearly a computer
docs.text:
The 1541 disk drive contained its own 6502-family processor and memory. This architecture descended from Commodore’s earlier IEEE-488 peripheral design: the drive was an intelligent device rather than a passive mechanism. It was flexible but notoriously slow in normal use, prompting fast-load cartridges and clever software loaders.

That tension is quintessentially Commodore. The machine offered startling capability for its price, but did not always organize that capability elegantly. Users learned workarounds; third parties sold improvements; the ecosystem became part of the product.

docs.title: Sound as a creative medium
docs.text:
SID’s filters, waveforms and modulation helped computer music become an art in its own right. Game composers developed techniques for suggesting percussion, arpeggiated chords and expressive lead lines with only three hardware voices. The chip’s distinctive character survived through demos, remixes, hardware synthesizers and modern software emulation.

The C64 was broad enough to be many first computers at once: game console, music machine, bulletin-board terminal, school tool, and programming laboratory.

docs.title: A platform made by its users
docs.text:
Commercial games dominate memory of the C64, but productivity programs, telecommunications, educational titles, public-domain disks and type-in listings mattered just as much. User groups traded knowledge before search engines existed. Modem owners called bulletin-board systems, one local phone call at a time. Demo coders pushed sprites, raster timing and sound far past the manufacturer’s polite examples.

The Commodore story links industrial strategy to creative culture. Cheap chips and mass distribution put millions of compatible machines into homes. People then discovered uses that no sales brochure could have specified.

Timeline anchor

The Computer History Museum dates the Commodore 64’s introduction to 1982. Its overview also notes that the 6502 family linked the C64 with systems as different as the Apple II, BBC Micro and Atari 800. See the CHM computer timeline.

Next: Atari brings arcade architecture home →

docs.title: Living with 8 bits
docs.text: Interlude · 9 minute read

docs.title: Living with 8 bits
docs.text: The experience of a home computer began before any software ran. It began by clearing space, negotiating for the television, finding the right lead, and deciding whether today the cassette recorder would cooperate.

docs.title: The shared screen
docs.text:
Many machines arrived without a display. That kept prices down but made the family television part of the system. Text could shimmer through an RF connection. Fine color patterns crawled. The computer was often packed away when someone wanted to watch a program.

Dedicated monitors transformed the experience but increased the cost and the space required. This difference shaped products: Apple and Atari sold flexible systems around optional displays; the PET and Amstrad packages made the screen part of the proposition; Sinclair and Commodore embraced the television.

docs.title: Waiting for tape
docs.text:
Cassettes made software distributable with existing, inexpensive technology. They also made loading a performance:

  1. Rewind to the counter number written on the inlay card.
  2. Type the load command.
  3. Press play.
  4. Watch borders, counters, or a loading screen for signs of progress.
  5. Discover, several minutes later, whether the process worked.

Different machines encoded data differently, and recording levels mattered. Owners cleaned heads, adjusted volume, duplicated tapes and learned to recognize the sound of data. A failed load was frustrating, but the audible process made storage strangely comprehensible.

docs.title: The book was part of the machine
docs.text:
Manuals assumed that a buyer might want to program. They explained variables, loops, graphics and sound, then offered projects. Magazines extended the manual every month. A listing might be a game, household database, drawing utility or demonstration of a machine-code routine.

Typing code created an unusual relationship with software. The reader became operator, copyist, debugger and—after changing a few lines—author. Errors taught syntax with little mercy. A semicolon could alter formatting; a transposed digit could hide for hours.

10 PRINT "WHAT IS YOUR NAME"; 20 INPUT N$ 30 PRINT "HELLO, ";N$ 40 GOTO 30 READY. RUN

docs.title: The computer club
docs.text:
Knowledge traveled socially. School friends swapped cassettes. User groups published newsletters and ran meetings. Shops employed enthusiasts who knew which cable or interface solved a problem. Bulletin-board systems connected modem users to messages and files, often within a local calling area.

These networks made fragmented platforms viable. If official documentation was thin, someone had mapped the memory. If a disk routine was slow, someone wrote a fast loader. If a game seemed impossible, a magazine printed a map.

docs.title: One computer, several identities
docs.text:
A single machine might spend the afternoon teaching fractions, the evening running a game, and the night dialing a bulletin board. The labels “educational,” “business,” and “games” described software shelves more neatly than household use.

That flexibility also explains the emotional force of “my first computer.” It was not merely an appliance with one job. It was a place—part toy box, part notebook, part workshop—whose boundaries expanded with each new disk, magazine, or discovered command.

Next: software, scenes and legacies →

docs.title: Software, scenes & legacies
docs.text: Chapter 09 · 9 minute read

docs.title: Software, scenes & legacies
docs.text: The hardware became obsolete. The practices did not. Home computers left behind ways of learning, publishing, composing and collaborating that remain visible in software culture.

docs.title: The bedroom route to publication
docs.text:
Low-cost machines and cassette distribution shortened the path from idea to audience. A programmer could write a game at home, duplicate it in small quantities, advertise in a magazine and sell by mail. Publishers professionalized the process, but the possibility of entry remained powerful.

The mythology of the lone “bedroom coder” can obscure artists, musicians, editors, duplicators, shopkeepers and collaborators. Even a one-person program depended on a network of tools and distribution. Still, the era demonstrated that software creation need not begin inside a large institution.

docs.title: Demos: software as performance
docs.text:
Cracking intros and demo scenes turned technical display into a competitive art. Code synchronized graphics with the raster beam, rearranged memory mid-frame, multiplexed sprites, synthesized music and exploited undocumented behavior. The point was not only what appeared on screen but the knowledge that the machine was supposedly unable to do it.

Platform differences created local dialects. Spectrum artists negotiated color attributes. C64 creators orchestrated VIC-II and SID. Atari programmers worked with display lists and player/missile graphics. Shared constraints produced recognizable styles without eliminating individual expression.

docs.title: The preservation stack
docs.text:
Preserving a home computer involves layers:

Hardware

Cases, boards, keyboards, power supplies and increasingly fragile custom chips.

Media

Cassettes, disks, cartridges, manuals, magazines, packaging and handwritten notes.

Software

Bit-accurate images, versions, copy protection, source code and documentation.

Context

Oral histories, broadcasts, advertisements, classrooms, clubs and everyday routines.

Emulation preserves repeatable access and supports research, but physical machines communicate scale, sound, latency, keyboard feel and setup friction. Neither substitutes perfectly for the other. Strong preservation treats them as complementary evidence.

docs.title: Why people return
docs.text:
Retro computing is sometimes described as nostalgia, but affection is only one entry point. These machines offer systems small enough to comprehend. Their limitations are productive. A complete program can fit in a few kilobytes; a graphics trick can be traced to specific registers; the boundary between software and hardware is unusually close.

Modern hardware projects, emulators, FPGA recreations and new software releases keep the platforms active. A forty-year-old machine can gain a storage adapter, network link, replacement video output or newly published game without ceasing to be historically interesting.

docs.title: What the era teaches
docs.text:
The home-computer boom offers no single recipe for good technology. Sinclair proved that price can create a public. Commodore showed how component control and distribution can build scale. Atari showed the expressive value of specialized hardware. Acorn joined media, curriculum and a capable machine. Apple demonstrated the compounding power of a compatible platform. TI exposed the gap between headline architecture and whole-system design. Amstrad made convenience a specification.

Their shared lesson is simpler: people become attached to computers that leave room for agency. A blinking cursor was an invitation.

docs.title: Help choose what comes next
docs.text:
This field guide is deliberately bounded, but its omissions need not remain invisible. Readers can suggest a focused addition, identify the gap it would fill and point to inspectable sources. GitHub reactions help indicate interest; evidence, scope, accessibility and editorial feasibility still decide what enters a production cycle.

docs.title: Sinclair — less is more
docs.text: Chapter 02 · 10 minute read

docs.title: Sinclair — less is more
docs.text: Sinclair’s early computers were arguments made in plastic: a computer did not need to be imposing, complete, or expensive. It needed to be just sufficient—and cheap enough to invite a risk.

docs.title: ZX80: the startling little machine
docs.text:
Introduced in 1980, the ZX80 compressed a Z80-based computer into a lightweight white case with a flat membrane keyboard. It connected to a television and used a domestic cassette recorder. It could be bought assembled or, for less, as a kit. The visual language was closer to a science-fiction prop than office equipment.

Its 1 KB of RAM made economy tangible. Display generation consumed processor time, so the screen blanked while the computer performed many operations. The keyboard offered BASIC keywords directly: press a key in the right mode and a whole command appeared. This saved memory and reduced typing, while giving the machine a distinctive grammar.

docs.title: ZX81: economy refined
docs.text:
The 1981 ZX81 looked like a black pebble beside its predecessor. A custom logic chip consolidated much of the ZX80’s circuitry, reducing component count and cost. The standard machine still had 1 KB of RAM, yet its low price turned an abstract interest in “computers” into a plausible household purchase.

1980ZX80Minimal, kit-friendly, visibly experimental. 1981ZX81Fewer chips, lower price, wider reach. 1982ZX SPECTRUMColor, sound and a software explosion.

The famous 16 KB RAM pack transformed what could be written, but its edge connector could be temperamental. A wobble might crash a program. Such stories matter because they capture the era’s bargain: extraordinary access accompanied by improvised ergonomics and fragile rituals.

docs.title: ZX Spectrum: constraints become identity
docs.text:
The ZX Spectrum added the features its name promised: color graphics, along with sound and substantially more memory in 16 KB and 48 KB versions. Rick Dickinson’s compact black case and rubber keys became an icon of British design. It was still unmistakably a Sinclair—small, cost-conscious, and attached to the family television—but it now supported a far richer software market.

The display system saved memory by applying color attributes to character-sized blocks rather than every pixel independently. When two differently colored objects occupied one block, their colors could clash. Programmers turned this technical compromise into a recognizable visual style through careful layout, dithering and monochrome sprites.

10 BORDER 0: PAPER 0: INK 6 20 FOR N=0 TO 21 30 PRINT AT N,N; "*" 40 NEXT N 50 GO TO 20

docs.title: A software culture in print
docs.text: Spectrum ownership meant more than commercial games. Magazines carried reviews, news, maps, hints, pokes, letters and type-in programs. Bedroom programmers could move from playing software to selling it with remarkably little infrastructure. Cassette duplication and mail order formed a low-cost path to market; specialist publishers and high-street retailers expanded it.

docs.title: Why the Spectrum endures
docs.text:
The machine’s limitations were legible. Owners knew why color behaved oddly, why loading took time, and why a program had to fit. That legibility encouraged experimentation. The Spectrum did not conceal the computer inside a smooth consumer experience. It placed the seams within reach.

In the collection

The Science Museum Group records the ZX80 as a 1980 microcomputer. The Computer History Museum’s timeline likewise places the ZX80 in 1980, followed by the mass-market expansion of the early 1980s. See the Science Museum object record and CHM timeline.

Next: Commodore builds for the masses →

docs.title: TI-99/4A — a 16-bit outlier
docs.text: Chapter 07 · 8 minute read

docs.title: TI-99/4A — a 16-bit outlier
docs.text:
The TI-99 family came from a company that made the chips inside other companies’ products. Its machine was technically distinctive, handsomely packaged, and constrained by choices that were difficult to explain on a shop floor.

Texas Instruments introduced the TI-99/4 in 1979 and the substantially improved TI-99/4A in 1981. The 4A’s silver-and-black console, full-travel keyboard and cartridge slot made it feel polished. Inside was the TMS9900, a 16-bit processor derived from TI’s minicomputer architecture.

docs.title: Sixteen bits—with detours
docs.text:
The “16-bit” label was real but incomplete as a measure of performance. Much of the system sat behind an 8-bit path, and the CPU’s directly accessible fast RAM was limited. Programs often moved through architectural bottlenecks to reach video memory and other resources. A specification that sounded decisive in an advertisement did not automatically make the machine faster than its rivals.

TMS990016-BIT CPU · ABOUT 3 MHZ 16 KBVIDEO RAM CartridgesINSTANT SOFTWARE, CONTROLLED FORMAT SpeechMEMORABLE OPTIONAL SYNTHESIZER

docs.title: The expansion box
docs.text:
Serious expansion arrived through the Peripheral Expansion Box, a substantial enclosure that could hold disk controllers, memory expansion, communications cards and other hardware. It turned the sleek console into the front end of a larger system—and made clear how much functionality lived outside the base unit.

The side-mounted speech synthesizer became the most charismatic accessory. Software could speak through a recognizable electronic voice, making educational programs and games feel futuristic. Speech was not merely a technical demo; it gave the machine a personality owners still remember.

docs.title: A closed ecosystem in a price war
docs.text:
TI controlled much of the software and cartridge ecosystem. That control could protect quality and support a coherent platform, but it also made third-party development harder than on some rivals. Meanwhile, competition with Commodore drove retail prices downward. The base computer became cheaper while a fully expanded system remained costly.

The TI-99/4A is a useful warning against histories written as simple races. It was neither “ahead” because its CPU was 16-bit nor irrelevant because the product line ended early. It offered a distinctive combination of industrial design, cartridge convenience, graphics, education and synthetic speech to a large community.

Historical anchor

The Computer History Museum records the original TI-99/4 in 1979, built around a 3 MHz TMS9900, and highlights its expansion system and popular speech synthesis. See the CHM timeline.

docs.title: TRS-80 Model I — computing on the high street
docs.text: Machine spotlight · 10 minute read

docs.title: TRS-80 Model I — computing on the high street
docs.text:
The TRS-80 Model I looked restrained beside its 1977 rivals. Its larger idea was not contained in the keyboard unit. Radio Shack presented the computer, display, storage, documentation, upgrades and retailer as parts of one system.

A plausible late-1977 retail demonstration: the TRS-80 system was a keyboard computer, monitor, cassette recorder and power supply arranged as one purchase. Original AI-generated editorial illustration; not an archival photograph or exact hardware reconstruction.

docs.title: A system in several boxes
docs.text:
Radio Shack introduced the TRS-80 Microcomputer System on 3 August 1977; “Model I” became its later name. The date is a reliable marker for the release, not proof that every shop had a machine ready for immediate collection. Radio Shack’s own brochure limited stock to selected stores as supplies allowed, so ordering, demonstrations and delivery could be separate moments. (Smithsonian; 1977 Radio Shack computer catalog, pp. 5–6)

The US launch package cost $599.95 in the period catalog. It brought together the keyboard computer, a 12-inch monitor and a CTR-41 cassette recorder, plus the power supply, an owner’s manual and a cassette of games. The quoted price belonged to the US offer and should not be generalized to other markets. A printer and floppy drive were future additions, not hidden inside that first bundle. (1977 Radio Shack computer catalog, pp. 2–4)

This was an appliance-like purchase without being an all-in-one appliance. The computer lived under the typist’s hands, the deep CRT sat behind it, and the recorder occupied more desk space alongside. What made the arrangement feel complete was not a single enclosure but the fact that the pieces had been selected and documented to work together.

docs.title: What four kilobytes invited
docs.text:
The launch machine used a Z80 processor running at about 1.77 MHz, with 4 KB of RAM, 4 KB of ROM and Level I BASIC. Its 53-key keyboard made the computer a programmable object rather than a board awaiting a terminal. The monochrome display could show 16 lines of 64 characters, switch to 32-column text, or arrange block graphics in a 128-by-48 field. (1977 Radio Shack computer catalog, pp. 3–4; TRS-80 Model I archive)

Those numbers describe a modest computer, but the bundle gave them a practical shape. Switch on and BASIC supplied the working environment. The dedicated monitor avoided tuning a family television. The external recorder made compact cassette the launch storage medium, under the computer’s control but still subject to the rewind-and-wait ritual of tape. Small memory encouraged short programs; saving them turned temporary experiments into possessions. The machine’s first invitation was therefore direct: type, run, save, revise.

Level I and Level II are easy to confuse with memory sizes because upgrades were often discussed together. Level II was a richer BASIC in 12 KB of ROM and supported 500-baud cassette operation; it was not simply “more RAM.” The computer could separately be expanded to 16 KB of internal RAM. Keeping ROM, RAM and language level distinct matters because the later disk system depended on a particular combination of them. (Level II BASIC archive)

docs.title: Expansion became a path
docs.text:
The Expansion Interface changed the scale of the system. It sat behind the keyboard, beneath the monitor, and connected to the computer by a short cable. Inside were two power supplies and space for additional RAM; externally it made room for two cassette connections, a printer, as many as four Mini-Disk drives and further bus expansion. An RS-232 serial board was optional rather than a standard port. A 16 KB Model I could reach 32 or 48 KB total through Interface memory. (Expansion Interface Manual, “Introduction” and “Capabilities and Advantages,” pp. 2–3; “Setting Up,” pp. 3–6; “Conclusion,” p. 6)

An expanded Model I arrangement: the monitor sits on the Expansion Interface, while cassette and disk remain distinct external additions. Original AI-generated editorial illustration; not an archival photograph or exact hardware reconstruction.

That list of connections mattered because it described a sequence of ownership. A buyer could begin with the launch cassette system, move to Level II and more memory, then add the Interface and disk rather than replace the original computer. The stack became less tidy as it became more capable, but the awkwardness was visible and purposeful: each added box turned the same keyboard unit into a larger system.

Disk was not a casual plug-in. Radio Shack’s 1978 Mini-Disk offer required a 16 KB machine, Level II BASIC and the Expansion Interface, and supplied TRSDOS and Disk BASIC. The catalog illustrated the payoff by claiming that a 13,000-byte program taking three and a half minutes to load from Level II cassette would load from disk in under twenty seconds. That is a manufacturer’s comparison, not an independent benchmark, but it captures the change in rhythm: storage could become part of an interactive working session rather than a long pause before it. (1978 Radio Shack computer catalog scan, “TRS-80 Mini-Disk System”; archival transcription, “TRS-80 Mini Disk System”)

Revision details set limits on this neat progression. The surviving 1979 Interface manual explicitly warns against connecting its documented version to a Level I machine. It is safer to describe the well-supported Level II disk configuration than to imply that every Interface revision worked with every early TRS-80. (Expansion Interface Manual, “Capabilities and Advantages,” p. 2; “Conclusion,” p. 6)

docs.title: The shop was part of the specification
docs.text:
Radio Shack’s launch brochure said the system could be ordered through more than 5,500 US stores and dealers and promised service through its stores. Both claims belong to the company and to 1977, but they reveal what it wanted the retail network to contribute. The shop could be a place to encounter the machine, order it, ask about accessories and return for support. That proximity was a feature even though it did not guarantee local stock or an identical experience at every counter. (1977 Radio Shack computer catalog, pp. 5–6)

This is where the Model I adds something distinct to the familiar 1977 trio. The PET concentrated computer, display and cassette into one enclosure. The Apple II left conspicuous space for internal cards. The TRS-80 made a supported base package and a staged chain of external additions legible through a consumer electronics retailer. Modest display capabilities did not make that surrounding system less important. For many uses, confidence that a machine could be found, expanded and serviced was as consequential as what it could draw.

docs.title: Model III: consolidation, not erasure
docs.text:
In 1980 the Model III gathered the monitor, a 65-key keyboard with data pad, and room for RAM, serial hardware and two disk drives into a self-contained case. The result consolidated a desk that the Model I had expanded in layers. Radio Shack said that “most” Model I software would run, a careful promise of continuity rather than full identity. (archived Model III description; Digital Design, October 1980, p. 59)

Compatibility had real limits, including differences between port and memory addresses. The Model III therefore belongs here as an afterlife, not as proof of an unbroken specification. It carried forward much of the Model I proposition while making the physical system more integrated. The Color Computer lies outside this chapter’s Model I–Model III scope.

docs.title: Object / Invitation / Afterlife
docs.text:
Object

A separate keyboard computer, 12-inch monitor and cassette recorder that could grow into a monitor-on-Interface stack with external disk drives.

Invitation

Begin with Level I BASIC and tape, then add language capability, memory, connections and faster storage as ambition and budget grew.

Afterlife

The Model III consolidated the expanding desk while preserving substantial—but not complete—Model I software continuity.
